methodological_rigor.justification: Population-based cohort study using high-quality SEER-21 cancer registry data covering 1.008 million cancer diagnoses (2015-2021). Appropriate statistical methods: cause-specific survival rates calculated using actuarial method; stage-specific trends fitted with proportional hazards models (JPSurv); absolute survival differences and mortality differences calculated. Stratified analyses by age, race/ethnicity, stage address potential confounding. Multiple imputation not required given registry completeness. Limitations acknowledged.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Population-based cohort study (2b) with high clinical relevance: first to quantify short-term survival impact of COVID-19 on newly diagnosed cancer patients. Demonstrates 17,390 excess cancer deaths (13.1% more than expected) within first year of diagnosis during 2020-2021. Direct impact on cancer care policy, monitoring, and health system resource allocation during and after future crises.

reporting_quality.justification: Well-reported observational study following STROBE guidelines. Clear presentation of data sources (SEER-21), inclusion/exclusion criteria, statistical methods, and results stratified by stage, demographics, and cancer site. SEER data are publicly available and regularly updated, supporting reproducibility. Limitations section addresses potential biases (cause-of-death misclassification, stage underestimation, loss to follow-up).

novelty_literature.justification: Novel application of existing surveillance data to quantify pandemic impact on cancer survival. While prior studies documented screening and diagnosis disruptions, this is first to measure short-term survival consequences. Uses established methodology (survival analysis, trend fitting) applied to new research question. Meaningful but incremental methodologic contribution.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with clear motivation, comprehensive methods, and informative results tables and figures. Kaplan-Meier-style survival curves communicate survival differences effectively. Discussion contextualizes findings within prior screening/diagnosis disruption literature. Strengths and limitations sections transparent about data quality and study design.

key_strengths: Large, high-quality population-based data (SEER-21, 1.008 million patients) ensures robust national estimates with external validity
Novel finding of 17,390 excess cancer deaths (13.1% more than expected) within first year quantifies pandemic impact on cancer outcomes
Comprehensive stratified analyses by stage, age, race/ethnicity, and cancer site identify vulnerable populations (elderly, other race/ethnicity, advanced stage)
Appropriate statistical methods: cause-specific survival to minimize COVID-related mortality misclassification; trend fitting accounts for stage distribution changes
Direct relevance to health policy and cancer care system preparedness for future disruptions
key_concerns: Cause-of-death classification may be imprecise during pandemic; reliance on death certificates could misattribute COVID-related deaths as cancer-specific
Short follow-up (maximum 12 months from diagnosis) may miss longer-term pandemic effects on survival
SEER-21 covers only ~41.9% of US population; geographic representation may not reflect all regions equally
Stage at diagnosis may be misclassified due to screening disruptions; stratified analyses attempt to address but residual confounding remains
Loss to follow-up (6.3% of 1 million patients) could bias survival estimates if non-random
chief_reviewer.rationale: Rigorous population-based study with novel finding of substantial pandemic impact on cancer survival. High clinical relevance for policy makers and oncologists. Appropriate methodology with transparent acknowledgment of limitations. Fits Tier 2 (solid methodology, clear translational relevance to health system planning). Data quality and national scope strengthen evidence for cancer care system resilience research.
